automatedSignalsProvision misdescribed proposed Art. 88b in three ways. (1) The article is limited by its title to 'processing of personal data in the terminal equipment of natural persons' (the cookie/ePrivacy rules moved into the GDPR). The summary presented it as a general machine-readable consent-and-objection duty. (2) The objection it covers is only the Art. 21(2) direct-marketing objection. (3) 'Once standards exist' comes from the explanatory memorandum. The operative text applies paragraphs 1-2 from a fixed date, 24 months after entry into force. Standards are requested separately and only give a presumption of conformity.

The record left out the part of Art. 88b that matters most for the MyTerms story: para. 6 would oblige web-browser providers that are not SMEs to provide the technical means for these machine-readable signals, 48 months after entry into force.

The record flagged the omnibus status as 'not independently verified'. fieldFixes.automatedSignalsProvision: Art. 21(5): in information-society services the data subject 'may exercise his or her right to object by automated means using technical specifications'. The Commission's Digital Omnibus proposal (COM(2025) 837, 19 Nov 2025) would add Art. 88b. It covers processing in people's terminal equipment (the cookie rules). Controllers' online interfaces would have to let people give consent, refuse it, and object to direct marketing (Art. 21(2)) 'through automated and machine-readable means', and would have to respect those choices, from 24 months after entry into force. European standards would be requested to interpret the signals. Web browsers from providers that are not SMEs would have to supply the technical means after 48 months. On 23 Sept 2026 the proposal (2025/0360(COD)) was still at committee stage in the European Parliament ('Awaiting committee decision').
fieldFixes.aiRules: AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (general application 2 Aug 2026). The 'Digital omnibus on AI' was adopted by the Council on 29 June 2026 and published as Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (OJ L, 24 July 2026). It moved high-risk obligations to 2 Dec 2027 for stand-alone systems and 2 Aug 2028 for AI embedded in products. GDPR Art. 22 separately limits decisions based solely on automated processing.

issues: All five quotes re-fetched from legislation.gov.uk and FOUND. They support the claims: the £17.5m/4% ceiling in Art. 83(5), the Art. 21(5) automated objection, Royal Assent on 19 June 2025, s.80 substituting Art. 22, and s.117 establishing the Information Commission.

The regulator field is out of date. It says the ICO is 'to be replaced' by the Information Commission. S.I. 2026/1015 (Commencement No. 9, made 10 Sept 2026) brings s.118 (abolition of the office of Information Commissioner) and s.119 (transfer of functions) into force on 30 September 2026. s.117 itself (except s.117(4)(a)) has been in force since 20 Aug 2025. So on 30 Sept 2026, one week after this was compiled, the regulator becomes the Information Commission.

aiRules does not say whether s.80 is in force. legislation.gov.uk records s.80 in force from 5 Feb 2026 (S.I. 2026/82), so Arts 22A-22D are current law, not prospective. It also omits a second restriction in new Art. 22B(4): no solely automated significant decision where processing relies on 'recognised legitimate interests' (Art. 6(1)(ea)).

Minor: Art. 21(5) does not keep the EU text word for word. The 'notwithstanding Directive 2002/58/EC' clause is replaced by a reference to 'domestic law made before IP completion day implementing Directive 2002/58/EC'. The automated-means wording itself is unchanged.

fieldFixes.regulator: Information Commissioner's Office until 29 Sept 2026. From 30 Sept 2026 the Information Commission, a corporate body set up by DUAA 2025 s.117, replaces it: the office of Information Commissioner is abolished and its functions are transferred (ss.118–119, commenced by S.I. 2026/1015).
fieldFixes.automatedSignalsProvision: UK GDPR Art. 21(5) keeps the EU rule that the data subject 'may exercise his or her right to object by automated means using technical specifications'. The only change is that the reference to the ePrivacy Directive now points to pre-exit domestic law implementing it.
fieldFixes.aiRules: No AI statute. DUAA 2025 s.80 (in force 5 Feb 2026) replaces UK GDPR Art. 22 with Arts. 22A–22D. Solely automated 'significant decisions' are allowed with safeguards, but they are restricted where special-category data are involved or where the processing relies on 'recognised legitimate interests' (Art. 6(1)(ea)).
fieldFixes.notes: DPA 2018 received Royal Assent in May 2018. The UK GDPR is the retained, amended text of the EU GDPR. DUAA 2025 received Royal Assent on 19 June 2025 and is being commenced in stages: s.80 from 5 Feb 2026, and the Information Commission replaces the ICO on 30 Sept 2026.

automatedSignalsProvision omitted the conditions attached to the duty. The controller 'shall comply' only if it can verify, with commercially reasonable effort, the consumer's identity and the agent's authority. It need not comply if the request is not clear and unambiguous, residency cannot be verified, the controller 'does not possess the ability to process the request', or it does not process similar requests under other states' laws. Rating 'yes' is kept, since there is a statutory duty, but the carve-outs are material and are now stated.

fieldFixes.automatedSignalsProvision: s.541.055(e), in force 1 Jan 2025: a consumer may designate an 'authorized agent' to opt out on their behalf 'using a technology', such as a browser setting or extension or a global device setting, so the statute treats the signal as an agent acting for the person. A controller 'shall comply' if it can verify, with commercially reasonable effort, the consumer's identity and the agent's authority. It need not comply if the request is unclear, Texas residency cannot be verified, it 'does not possess the ability to process the request', or it does not process similar requests under other states' laws.
